panels.title: Request Export Latency

panels.description: Average number of clients queued for a server connection, per pooler. Integrated from PgBouncer's cumulative wait time, so unlike the instantaneous cl_waiting it cannot miss queueing between scrapes. Sustained non-zero means that pool is saturated: every queued client is a round trip waiting on someone else's transaction (database.md section 7).
panels.title: Clients Waiting for a Server

panels.description: Average time a transaction waited for a server connection before it could start, per pooler. This is the latency the pool adds to every query from that pooler's clients.

targets.expr: sum by (pooler) (rate(cnpg_pgbouncer_stats_total_wait_time{namespace=~"$namespace", database="app"}[$__rate_interval])) / sum by (pooler) (rate(cnpg_pgbouncer_stats_total_xact_count{namespace=~"$namespace", database="app"}[$__rate_interval])) / 1e6

panels.title: Mean Pool Wait per Transaction

panels.description: How long the oldest currently queued client has been waiting, per pooler (the worst pod). A rising line is a queue that is not draining.
panels.title: Longest Client Wait

panels.description: Server connections running a transaction, per pooler, summed over its pods. A flat line at default_pool_size x pods (prod rw: 25 x 2 = 50) is a full pool. rw, api and tasks draw on the primary's max_connections; ro on the replicas'.
panels.title: Server Connections in Use

panels.description: Transactions completed through each pooler. The denominator for the wait panels above: a pool can queue because its clients got slower or because there are more of them.
panels.title: Transactions per Second

panels.description: Actual connections held open against Postgres itself.
panels.title: PostgreSQL Backends

panels.description: Tasks published and waiting for a worker to pick them up. A flat non-zero line on background means the queue is not draining. RabbitMQ reports a queue only from the node hosting it, so this is a max across nodes rather than a sum. Extract tasks no longer go through RabbitMQ, so processing stays empty.
panels.title: Celery Queue Depth (Ready)

panels.description: Tasks handed to a worker but not yet acknowledged, i.e. running. Celery acks late, so this tracks concurrency in use. It is capped by worker replicas x concurrency; sitting at that ceiling while Ready climbs is the signal to scale workers out.
panels.title: Celery Tasks In Flight (Unacked)

panels.description: Worker processes subscribed to each queue. Dropping to zero means nothing is serving that queue, which looks identical to an idle system on the depth panels until work arrives and stays.
panels.title: Celery Consumers per Queue

panels.description: Extract tasks finished per second across the processing workers. completed and failed are the task's own result; unavailable means the row was no longer claimable when the worker reached it; error is an exception before the row was locked.
panels.title: Extract Tasks/sec by Outcome

panels.description: Datasets completing the most extract tasks per second. Picked per point, so more than ten can appear over a long range.
panels.title: Completed Tasks/sec – Top 10 Datasets

panels.description: Average wall time one task spends in each phase; the stack's height is the mean task duration. lock = select and mark the row running; load = resource, geometry and category map lookups; extract = processor calls (raster I/O and compute); write = build and store extract_data rows; finalize = the terminal status update.
panels.title: Mean Seconds per Task by Phase

panels.description: Fraction of each phase's wall time spent on CPU in the worker process. Low means the phase is waiting on the database or disk; near 100% means it is compute-bound.
panels.title: CPU Share per Phase

panels.description: Worker slots, by what they are doing: running tasks, claiming the next chunk (claim lock wait and claim), or idle between chunks (including the wait after finding the queue empty). The stack should come to roughly the fleet's slot count (replicas × concurrency); a shortfall is time none of these cover, such as releasing a chunk, closing connections, or worker processes being recycled.
panels.title: Where Slot Time Goes

panels.description: Fraction of time the fleet-wide claim lock is held by a processing worker's claim. Near 100%, the claim is the throughput ceiling and more slots will only add lock wait; raise claimBatch so each claim takes more tasks. The dashed line marks 90%, above which the claim is likely limiting throughput.
panels.title: Claim Lock Utilization

panels.description: Time a worker waits to acquire the fleet-wide claim lock, including any wait for a pooler connection.
panels.title: Claim Lock Wait

panels.description: Time a worker process waits between finishing one chunk and claiming the next. Normally near zero; a slot that found the queue empty waits about EXTRACT_WORKER_IDLE_SECONDS (60s by default) before claiming again.
panels.title: Slot Idle Gap

panels.description: Wall time from claiming a chunk of extract tasks to finishing or releasing all of it. The chunk's rows sit in status 2 that long, and free_stale_processing_tasks returns them to pending after STALE_TASK_MINUTES (30), after which they run twice. Yellow from 15 minutes, red from 25: lower the processing claimBatch before it gets there. max is the upper bound of the highest bucket that saw a chunk.
panels.title: Chunk Duration

panels.description: WAL written by the primary. This is the cluster's write load: every replica replays it and the archiver ships it.
panels.title: WAL Generated

panels.description: All WAL divided by extract tasks completed: the database write cost of one unit of useful work, comparable across throughput levels. It includes the builder's inserts and request builds, so it rises when the builder runs. database.md recorded 2.8-3.9 KB.
panels.title: WAL per Completed Task

panels.description: Full-page images written to WAL per completed task. Each checkpoint makes the next touch of every page log the whole 8 kB page, so this spikes after checkpoints and climbs when they come too often (database.md section 10).
panels.title: Full-Page Images per Completed Task

panels.description: Checkpoints on the primary. timed are the scheduled ones (checkpoint_timeout); requested were forced by WAL volume reaching max_wal_size, and write flat out regardless of checkpoint_completion_target. Requested should stay near zero: a sustained share of them is the self-reinforcing checkpoint/full-page-image loop in database.md section 10.
panels.title: Checkpoints in the Trailing Hour

panels.description: What client backends on the primary are doing, sampled at each scrape. CPU / Running means executing, not waiting. LWLock WALWrite and IO WALSync are the write path's storage bandwidth; Lock and advisory are row or claim-lock contention; Client ClientRead in an idle in transaction state is a pooler slot held while the client does something else. Check this before optimising anything (database.md, Working rules).

targets.expr: sum by (wait_event_type, wait_event) (cnpg_geoquery_wait_events_backends{namespace=~"$namespace"} and on(namespace, pod) (cnpg_pg_replication_in_recovery{namespace=~"$namespace"} == 0))

panels.title: Primary Backends by Wait Event

panels.description: Rows written per second, summed over partitions. tasks created is the builder plus request materialization; task updates are about three per processed task (claim, start, finish); extract_data rows are processing's results.
panels.title: Partitioned Table Row Writes

panels.description: Row updates on extract_tasks per completed task. A processed task is updated three times (0->3 claim, 3->2 start, 2->1 finish), so this should sit near 3. Above that, sweeps are resetting stranded or errored tasks, which then run again.
panels.title: extract_tasks Updates per Completed Task

panels.description: Share of extract_tasks updates that were heap-only (rewrote no index entries). Expected to be about zero: status appears in the partial claim index's predicate, which rules HOT out for every status change (database.md section 3). A change here means the index set changed.
panels.title: extract_tasks HOT Update Ratio

panels.description: Bytes of table and index data written out of shared buffers on the primary, by process type. checkpointer and background writer are the normal path. client backend writes mean queries are evicting dirty buffers themselves, on their own time.
panels.title: Primary Relation Writes by Process

panels.description: Heap and index bytes of extract_tasks and extract_data, summed over partitions.
panels.title: Partitioned Table Size

panels.description: Estimated dead row versions, summed over partitions. Every extract_tasks update leaves one behind; this should saw-tooth as autovacuum keeps up, not climb.
panels.title: Dead Rows Awaiting Vacuum

targets.expr: topk(15, sum by (query) (rate(cnpg_geoquery_statements_exec_seconds{namespace=~"$namespace"}[$__range]) and on(namespace, pod) (cnpg_pg_replication_in_recovery{namespace=~"$namespace"} == 0)))

sum by (query) (rate(cnpg_geoquery_statements_calls{namespace=~"$namespace"}[$__range]) and on(namespace, pod) (cnpg_pg_replication_in_recovery{namespace=~"$namespace"} == 0)) and on(query) topk(15, sum by (query) (rate(cnpg_geoquery_statements_exec_seconds{namespace=~"$namespace"}[$__range]) and on(namespace, pod) (cnpg_pg_replication_in_recovery{namespace=~"$namespace"} == 0)))

(topk(15, sum by (query) (rate(cnpg_geoquery_statements_exec_seconds{namespace=~"$namespace"}[$__range]) and on(namespace, pod) (cnpg_pg_replication_in_recovery{namespace=~"$namespace"} == 0)))) / (sum by (query) (rate(cnpg_geoquery_statements_calls{namespace=~"$namespace"}[$__range]) and on(namespace, pod) (cnpg_pg_replication_in_recovery{namespace=~"$namespace"} == 0))) * 1000

panels.title: Top Statements on the Primary
panels.description: The statements with the most cumulative execution time on the primary over the selected range, from pg_stat_statements. Load is execution seconds per second: the average number of backends busy running that statement. Only each instance's current top 20 is exported, so a statement new to the list shows less than its full range.

Extract tasks created (the builder plus request materialization) against tasks completed by processing. Completed persistently above created means processing is waiting on the builder; the reverse means the backlog is growing.
panels.title: Tasks Created vs Completed per Hour

panels.description: Rows in each status-filtered partial index on extract_tasks. An estimate from pg_class, refreshed as autovacuum visits each partition, so it moves in steps and trails reality by up to one autovacuum cycle; an exact count would scan every pending row on each scrape. Log scale: pending is millions, in flight is about the fleet's slot count times the batch size, and errored is usually a handful.
panels.title: Tasks by State (estimated)

panels.description: Requests not yet complete or failed. 4 = creating its extract tasks, -1 = tasks created, awaiting its first sweep, 0 = waiting on its tasks, 2 = a sweep is building its output.
panels.title: Open Requests by Status

panels.description: Age since submission of the oldest request in each open status. Statuses 4 and 2 are normal transient states, so a request stranded in one looks like any other unless its age is watched; database.md section 8 records one that sat at 4 for four days.
panels.title: Oldest Open Request
